title: 05 - Rights

content.text: Syllabus — Rights: meaning and theories; different kinds of rights; concept of Human Rights. (UPSC PSIR Paper-1A, Unit 5)

the meaning, nature and theories of rights (natural, legal, moral, conservative/historical, social-welfare, Marxist, and contemporary — libertarian, communitarian, multicultural); types of rights and the negative/positive distinction; the doctrine of ‘rights as trumps’; and human rights — the three generations, the ‘Asian values’ critique, and the universalism vs cultural-relativism debate.
Laski, Locke, Paine, Bentham, Burke, T.H. Green, Kant, Dworkin, Joseph Raz, Nozick, Walzer, Kymlicka, Bhikhu Parekh, Karel Vasak, Lee Kuan Yew, Isaiah Berlin, Susan Moller Okin, Amartya Sen.

Q — Critically examine the theories of rights — natural, legal, moral, conservative/historical, social-welfare and Marxist. ‘Idea of natural rights.’ Comment. (UPSC 2015)
Define a right → run through the rival theories of where rights come from → judge which account survives.

(A child without schooling can never develop her powers — hence Art 21A.)
the state, so the state only recognises them.
(The 1776 American Declaration’s ‘self-evident’ life, liberty and the pursuit of happiness — no legislature conferred them.)

(You may vote at 18 only because the Constitution’s 61st Amendment says so — not because nature says so.)
— rights from reason and moral personality (
(But custom also sanctioned sati and untouchability — which is why India abolished them by law.)
— rights are justified by the common good (
(A bonded labourer has a legal right to freedom yet no means to use it.)
social-democratic synthesis: ‘every state is known by the rights it maintains’.

defines rights as “those conditions of social life without which no man can seek, in general, to be himself at his best” — a child denied schooling can never develop her powers, which is why India made elementary education a fundamental right under Article 21A. A right is thus a claim recognised by society, and historically a
concept that replaced the divine right of kings by limiting the power of state and society. The rival theories differ chiefly on the
The 17th–18th century doctrine treats rights as a corollary of
— inherent in human nature, held before and independently of the state, which merely recognises them.
(life, liberty and property) is its champion, and

gives it a teleological basis. Its power is visible in the ‘self-evident truths’ of the American Declaration (1776) and the French Declaration (1789), and in modern courts reading unenumerated rights into constitutional texts. Its weakness is that ‘nature’ supplies no agreed list and no enforcement.
is the real source, for ‘real laws give birth to real rights’, and rights claimed against the law are
and ‘anarchical fallacies’. The point is concrete: an Indian citizen votes at eighteen only because the 61st Amendment lowered the age, not because nature ordained it.

refines the position — a legal right is ‘an interest recognised and protected by the rule of law’, enforceable by a determinate authority. The criticism is that a purely legal theory leaves the citizen defenceless against an unjust law.

) derives rights from the dictates of reason and moral personality — persons must be treated ‘as ends, never merely as means’ — so a right exists wherever it is a condition of moral self-realisation, even if unenforced. The
grounds rights instead in a long process of

and prescription; he condemned the French Revolution’s ‘metaphysical abstractions’ in favour of ‘the rights of Englishmen’. The standing reply is Indian: custom equally sanctioned sati and untouchability, abolished only by deliberate legislation and Articles 17 and 15.
theory — Bentham’s utilitarian legacy carried forward by
— holds that rights are justified only in so far as they serve the ‘greatest happiness’ and the common good; critics find the standard vague and majoritarian. The

view is sharper: rights are a ‘bourgeois concept’, class law lodged in the superstructure, conferring formal liberty without substantive power — the bonded labourer holds a legal right to freedom yet lacks the means to exercise it, so genuine rights require the abolition of class division.

social-democratic synthesis best reconciles the traditions: rights are rooted in social good yet must secure both individual liberty and social justice, uniting the moral force of natural rights with the enforceability of legal rights. His maxim that ‘every state is known by the rights it maintains’ remains the working test of any regime.
Q — Discuss the doctrine of ‘rights as trumps’ (Dworkin) and its critics. Can the right to privacy trump state interest? (UPSC 2019)
Explain what ‘trumps’ means → apply it to privacy → test it against Dworkin’s own exceptions and his critics.
that beat collective goals, as a trump card beats any other suit.
(Privacy cannot be overridden merely because a database is administratively convenient.)
between a right and a policy benefit; rights are not state gifts.
(Majority welfare cannot license torturing one suspect.)
— a right sets the limit policy must respect.
(Puttaswamy, 2017: nine judges read privacy into Art 21, so surveillance must clear legality, necessity and proportionality — not mere ‘security’ assertion.)
— only where the right is at stake in an
— utilitarians deny the priority of rights over aggregate welfare;
— rights are near-absolute, not absolute: a via media between rigid absolutism and utilitarian expediency.
argues that individual rights function as

— as a trump card defeats any card of another suit, a right defeats the collective goals of the community or state. Rights are not what the state chooses to grant; on the contrary ‘the sole purpose of the state is the maintenance of rights’. Hence privacy cannot be overridden merely because a centralised database would be administratively convenient.
The doctrine is directed against the
view that a person is entitled only to what the state confers, and that any right may be balanced away once aggregate welfare rises. On the trumps model there is

: a genuine right cannot be defeated simply because its violation maximises utility, which is why majority benefit cannot license torturing a single suspect. Rights, for Dworkin, express the government’s duty of ‘equal concern and respect’ for each person.
cannot ordinarily be trumped by a bare appeal to national security or efficiency; the right fixes the boundary within which policy must operate. India supplies the sharpest illustration: in
K.S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India (2017)

a nine-judge Bench held privacy intrinsic to the right to life under Article 21, so state intrusion must satisfy legality, necessity and proportionality. That test is the trumps doctrine in institutional form — the state must justify the intrusion, not the citizen the right.
Dworkin concedes that a right may be compromised in two narrow cases: first, where the value the right protects is at stake only in some
of honouring it is grossly disproportionate to its benefit — as with limited disclosure of movement data during an epidemic.

reasons similarly that even human dignity, though it normally prevails, may be ‘partially defeated’ in unavoidable circumstances. The exceptions are principled limits, not a general balancing licence.
Utilitarians reject any lexical priority of rights over aggregate welfare, arguing that Dworkin smuggles in an unargued moral hierarchy.
, holds that law is ‘autonomous’ — there is no necessary continuity between legal rights and morality — while communitarians such as
object that the rights-bearing individual is abstracted from the community that gives rights their meaning.

‘Rights as trumps’ remains the strongest defence of the individual against majoritarian and executive overreach, and it has shaped judicial review far beyond the Anglo-American world. Its qualified exceptions show that even Dworkin treats rights as near-absolute rather than wholly absolute — a via media between rigid absolutism and utilitarian expediency.
Q — Can there be a universal conception of human rights? Examine the debate between universalism and cultural relativism. (UPSC 2021)
State what human rights claim → give the case for universality → present the relativist attack → arrive at a defensible middle position.
— post-1945 claims held by all persons simply as human, codified in the
(UDHR 1948, drafted in reaction to Nazi atrocities, plus the two 1966 Covenants.)
(Echoed in the Indian Preamble’s promise of ‘dignity of the individual’.)
— a common humanity gives an equal, inalienable claim, and it has abolished manifestly inhuman practices.
(Sati, banned in 1829 after Raja Ram Mohan Roy; female foeticide; genital mutilation — no culture may plead custom.)
(The 1993 Bangkok Declaration’s plea for ‘national and regional peculiarities’; the ‘Asian values’ school.)
, so no culture may rank another’s.
(Liberty and equality both matter, yet more of one costs the other.)
‘dialogue among civilisations’, not imposed at gunpoint.

Human rights are claims held by every person ‘just because they are human’, irrespective of state, race or creed. They emerged after the Second World War in reaction to the Nazi atrocities and were codified in the

together with the two 1966 Covenants on Civil and Political and on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights. Their novelty lies in piercing sovereignty: how a state treats its own citizens becomes a matter of international concern.
natural rights — the ‘self-evident truths’ that survive the transfer to civil society — to
, by which every person is an end in himself and never merely a means. From this follows their defining and most contested attribute,
: rights are equal, inalienable and permanent. The Indian Preamble’s pledge to secure ‘the dignity of the individual’ shows how deeply the Kantian premise travelled into post-colonial constitutions.

If humanity is one, a claim grounded in humanity alone cannot stop at borders. The practical vindication is that universal standards have delivered where local custom would not: sati, defended as tradition, was banned in 1829 after the campaign of

; female foeticide and genital mutilation are today indefensible on cultural grounds; and the corpus keeps expanding, as with the United Nations’ recognition of a human right to water. Without a universal core, the victims of majoritarian custom would have no vocabulary of appeal.
— the concept descends from the anthropologist
— hold that every culture is rational on its own terms and that no hierarchy of cultures exists.
add that the self is ‘situated’ and constituted by community, so an abstract rights-bearer is a fiction. Together they charge that ‘universal’ rights are in fact
, stressing ‘national and regional peculiarities’, gave the objection diplomatic form.
deepens the difficulty: values are genuinely

— liberty and equality are both authentic goods, yet more of one is bought at the cost of the other, and there is ‘no objective criterion’ for ranking them. The West is therefore not entitled to impose its own ordering. Yet Berlin does not collapse into relativism: he retains certain ‘generic values’ common to humanity and prizes
— Voltaire’s ‘I detest what you say, yet will defend your right to say it’.
A universal conception is defensible, but only as a
of human dignity — against torture, slavery, genocide and arbitrary killing — whose content is enlarged through
‘dialogue among civilisations’ rather than imposed ‘at gunpoint’. Human rights should thus be universal in their core and plural in their expression.
Q — What do you understand by the three generations of human rights? (UPSC 2018)
Explain Vasak’s classification generation by generation, and bring out the negative/positive distinction that underlies it.
(1979, Strasbourg) classified human rights on the French Revolution’s
(The state may not censor a newspaper — Art 19(1)(a); ICCPR 1966.)
: the state MUST act and spend.
(The state must provide free schooling to every 6–14 year-old — Art 21A and the RTE Act, 2009; ICESCR 1966.)
(A healthy environment, development, peace — as in the climate-finance claims of the Global South.)
— negative vs positive rights; welfare states combine both.
(India: enforceable Part III rights beside non-justiciable Part IV directives, later judicially fused through Art 21.)
— the generations chart a widening of rights, but the sequence metaphor wrongly implies the later ones are less urgent.
The ‘three generations’ framework was proposed in

at the International Institute of Human Rights, Strasbourg. He classified the growing corpus of human rights along the lines of the French Revolution’s slogan ‘liberty, equality, fraternity’, each generation corresponding to a historical phase in which a new kind of claim was pressed and a different demand was made upon the state.
2. First generation — civil and political rights.
, these are the liberal rights of life, liberty, property, equality before law, freedom of expression, conscience and the vote, recognised in the 1966 Covenant on Civil and Political Rights. They are
in form: they succeed by the state’s

, not its exertion — the state must NOT censor a newspaper, arrest without warrant or bar a person from a public office. Article 19(1)(a) of the Indian Constitution is enforceable precisely because it demands abstention, which costs the treasury nothing.
3. Second generation — socio-economic and cultural rights.
and championed by socialist states, these cover work, fair wages, social security, health and education, and were recognised in the 1966 Covenant on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights. They are

: they require the state to build, employ and spend. India’s Article 21A read with the Right to Education Act, 2009 obliges the state to provide free and compulsory schooling to every child aged six to fourteen — a duty of provision, not of restraint. Both the first and second generations remain

claims ‘exercised in solidarity’ — self-determination, peace, development, a healthy environment, humanitarian assistance and a share in the common heritage of mankind. Their bearer is a people rather than a person, and their duty-holder is the international community: the Global South’s demand for climate finance and technology transfer, resting on common but differentiated responsibility, is a third-generation claim in action.
Cutting across the generations is the

between freedom from interference and freedom to realise oneself. Negative rights are cheap, judicially enforceable and immediate; positive rights are costly, progressive and politically contested. The modern welfare state combines both, and India illustrates the fusion — justiciable fundamental rights in Part III alongside non-justiciable Directive Principles in Part IV, which the Supreme Court has progressively read into Article 21 as rights to livelihood, health and a clean environment.
The generations map the historical widening of rights: from the individual
the state, to the individual’s welfare

the state, to humanity’s shared claims beyond the state. The metaphor must not be pressed too far, however — treating them as a sequence wrongly implies the later generations are derivative or less urgent, whereas the Vienna Declaration (1993) affirms that all human rights are indivisible and interdependent.
Q — Critically examine the ‘Asian values’ critique of human rights and the challenges to their implementation. (UPSC 2016)
Set out what the Asian-values school claims → explain why enforcement is hard → assess how far the critique holds.

— rights are not universal; society is

pressed ‘national and regional peculiarities’ before the Vienna World Conference.

yet states are their only guardians, so enforcement means
(UN bodies can name and shame, but cannot enter a sovereign jurisdiction.)

The ‘Asian values’ critique arose in the 1990s, after the collapse of the USSR left liberal rights apparently unchallenged and the rise of East Asia supplied a rival model of development. Its principal proponents,
of Malaysia, traced their position to

, which prizes social harmony, hierarchy and duty to the group above the assertion of individual claims — Singapore’s combination of high prosperity with tightly limited dissent being offered as proof of concept.
The school advances four propositions: first, human rights are
and cannot be globalised, since they grew from a specific Western history; second, Asian societies are centred on the
rather than the atomised individual; third,
— food, housing, employment — rank above political rights for poor societies, so ‘feed the people first, elections later’; and fourth,
includes domestic jurisdiction over one’s human-rights record, so other nations should not interfere.
These claims were not merely academic. At the regional meeting preceding the Vienna World Conference on Human Rights, the

affirmed the universality of human rights in principle while insisting that their implementation ‘must bear in mind the significance of national and regional peculiarities and various historical, cultural and religious backgrounds’ — an attempt to convert cultural relativism into a norm of international law.
Post-colonial and cultural-relativist thinkers reinforce the critique, reading the universal human-rights regime as

— the successor to the civilising mission, now deployed selectively against weaker states. The Western rejoinder is that Asian values amount to ‘soft authoritarianism’: a doctrine articulated by ruling elites rather than by peoples, and used to justify episodes such as the suppression at Tiananmen in 1989 or the silencing of opposition media.
The deeper difficulty is structural. Human rights are inherently
— they are claims against power — yet states remain their principal guardians, so governments offer ‘moral guarantees’ that they routinely fail to honour. Enforcement therefore becomes ‘a matter of

’, which sovereignty, the non-interference claim and the absence of coercive machinery all resist. International bodies can monitor, report and shame; beyond that, compliance depends on domestic courts, a free press and civil society.
offers the decisive rebuttal: Asia contains sixty per cent of humanity and an immense diversity of traditions, so there is no single ‘Asian value’; and freedom is not un-Asian — in
he cites Ashoka’s edicts on toleration and Akbar’s

as indigenous roots of liberty. The critique rightly warns against ethnocentric imposition, but hardens into a shield for authoritarian denial; the way forward is a negotiated basic minimum, monitored internationally yet advanced through dialogue rather than coercion.
Q — Discuss multiculturalism and minority rights, with special reference to Kymlicka and Bhikhu Parekh.
Explain why equal treatment may require unequal rights → give Kymlicka’s and Parekh’s schemes → weigh the feminist and liberal objections.
— grew out of the liberal–communitarian debate: identity is culturally embedded, so identical treatment can entrench disadvantage.
(A uniform dress code silently excludes a turbaned Sikh.)

(personal laws can shield unequal maintenance or inheritance)
— accommodate difference, but bound it by a basic minimum of individual rights.

. Its premise is that culture is constitutive of identity and of the range of options from which a person chooses, so a formally neutral rule may in practice impose the majority’s culture — a uniform dress code or a Sunday holiday silently excludes the turbaned Sikh or the observant minority worker. Treating people as equals may therefore require not identical but
, argues that liberalism itself requires the protection of minority cultures, because a secure ‘societal culture’ is the context within which meaningful choice, and hence
, is possible. Being born into a vulnerable minority culture is ‘bad brute luck’ rather than a chosen disadvantage, and on his
premise the state owes its rectification. Multiculturalism is thus a completion of liberalism, not a departure from it.

protect distinctive religious and cultural practice — Articles 29 and 30 of the Indian Constitution permit minorities to conserve their script and to establish and administer their own educational institutions.
secure a political voice, as with reserved seats for Scheduled Castes and Tribes under Articles 330 and 332.

grant territorial autonomy, exemplified by the Fifth and Sixth Schedules with their autonomous district councils in the North-East. Crucially, he reserves the last for ‘national minorities’ incorporated involuntarily, not for voluntary immigrants.

, takes a post-colonial position: multiculturalism is the ‘creative interplay’ of cultural embeddedness and human plurality, and no culture is complete in itself. He finds no logic in denying special rights to non-citizen minorities, applies a
to test contested cultural practices rather than banning them wholesale, and insists that universal principles must be constructed through
, anchored in the shared value of
Feminists warn that protecting cultures can entrench patriarchy:

‘multiculturalism is bad for women’ argues that group rights typically empower male elders, and India’s personal-law debates over maintenance and inheritance illustrate the risk of internal minorities being sacrificed to external protection. Liberals such as
fear ‘ghettoisation’ and ‘plural monoculturalism’ — communities living side by side rather than together — with a corresponding weakening of shared citizenship.

Multiculturalism corrects the blindness of abstract equal treatment and is indispensable in deeply diverse societies such as India. But it must be bounded: group rights are legitimate as external protections against majority pressure, not as internal restrictions on dissenting members, so cultural accommodation must stop at the basic minimum of individual human rights.
Q — Assess the significance of the right to property in political theory. (UPSC 2020)
Trace why property is the most contested right — the liberal defence, the socialist attack, the social-liberal balance — and what its Indian career proves.

(Zamindari: title for one, tenancy for millions.)

right (Art 300A) so land reform could proceed — property is conditional, not absolute.
Few rights have divided political theory as sharply as the right to property, precisely because it stands at the crossroads of

. As a bulwark of independence it shields the individual from the state; as an accumulation of power it reproduces inequality across generations. Colonial India furnishes the illustration: the permanent settlement created secure proprietary title for the zamindar and precarious tenancy for millions, so the same right simultaneously guaranteed freedom and entrenched subordination.

replied that private ownership is a school of virtue — it teaches prudence, liberality and responsibility, and what is common to all is cared for by none.

defended it on utilitarian grounds as the indispensable engine of incentive, security and social progress, an argument echoed today in evidence that secure land titling raises investment.

rather than an absolute claim, while
— no fortune is the product of one man’s effort alone, since it presupposes law, infrastructure and society’s cooperation, which justifies taxation and redistribution.

makes the owner a custodian holding wealth for society.

India’s constitutional history is the clearest practical judgment on the question. Property began as a fundamental right under Articles 19(1)(f) and 31, but the collision between land reform and compensation produced a long duel between Parliament and the Supreme Court, resolved by the
, which deleted Article 31 and relocated property as a

. The significance of the right to property therefore lies in this unresolved tension — indispensable to individual freedom yet dangerous to equality — which is why the modern welfare state treats it not as absolute but as socially conditioned.

contentText: Syllabus — Rights: meaning and theories; different kinds of rights; concept of Human Rights. (UPSC PSIR Paper-1A, Unit 5) Unit Snapshot What this unit covers:  the meaning, nature and theories of rights (natural, legal, moral, conservative/historical, social-welfare, Marxist, and contemporary — libertarian, communitarian, multicultural); types of rights and the negative/positive distinction; the doctrine of ‘rights as trumps’; and human rights — the three generations, the ‘Asian values’ critique, and the universalism vs cultural-relativism debate. Must-know thinkers:  Laski, Locke, Paine, Bentham, Burke, T.H. Green, Kant, Dworkin, Joseph Raz, Nozick, Walzer, Kymlicka, Bhikhu Parekh, Karel Vasak, Lee Kuan Yew, Isaiah Berlin, Susan Moller Okin, Amartya Sen. PYQ trend:  universal conception of human rights (2021), right to property (2020), rights as trumps (2019), three generations (2018), implementation/changing conduct of states (2016), natural rights (2015). Master Questions Q — Critically examine the theories of rights — natural, legal, moral, conservative/historical, social-welfare and Marxist. ‘Idea of natural rights.’ Comment. (UPSC 2015) What it’s asking:  Define a right → run through the rival theories of where rights come from → judge which account survives. Gist — the spine to recall 1. Meaning  — a right is a condition of social life needed to be one’s best self, and it is originally  anti-statist .  (A child without schooling can never develop her powers — hence Art 21A.)  —  Laski . 2. Natural rights  — rights flow from natural law,  prior to  the state, so the state only recognises them.  (The 1776 American Declaration’s ‘self-evident’ life, liberty and the pursuit of happiness — no legislature conferred them.)  —  Locke ,  Paine . 3. Legal rights  — only the state creates rights; natural rights are  ‘nonsense upon stilts’ .  (You may vote at 18 only because the Constitution’s 61st Amendment says so — not because nature says so.)  —  Bentham ,  Salmond . 4. Moral & conservative  — rights from reason and moral personality ( Kant, Green ) versus rights as inherited  custom  ( Burke ).  (But custom also sanctioned sati and untouchability — which is why India abolished them by law.) 5. Social-welfare & Marxist  — rights are justified by the common good ( Bentham, Pound ), or exposed as a  ‘bourgeois concept’ .  (A bonded labourer has a legal right to freedom yet no means to use it.) 6. Conclusion  —  Laski’s  social-democratic synthesis: ‘every state is known by the rights it maintains’. Model Answer 1. Meaning.  Harold Laski  defines rights as “those conditions of social life without which no man can seek, in general, to be himself at his best” — a child denied schooling can never develop her powers, which is why India made elementary education a fundamental right under Article 21A. A right is thus a claim recognised by society, and historically a  modern, anti-statist  concept that replaced the divine right of kings by limiting the power of state and society. The rival theories differ chiefly on the  source  of that claim. 2. Natural rights.  The 17th–18th century doctrine treats rights as a corollary of  natural law  — inherent in human nature, held before and independently of the state, which merely recognises them.  John Locke  (life, liberty and property) is its champion, and  Tom Paine  in  Rights of Man  gives it a teleological basis. Its power is visible in the ‘self-evident truths’ of the American Declaration (1776) and the French Declaration (1789), and in modern courts reading unenumerated rights into constitutional texts. Its weakness is that ‘nature’ supplies no agreed list and no enforcement. 3. Legal rights.  Jeremy Bentham  reverses this: the  state  is the real source, for ‘real laws give birth to real rights’, and rights claimed against the law are  “nonsense upon stilts”  and ‘anarchical fallacies’. The point is concrete: an Indian citizen votes at eighteen only because the 61st Amendment lowered the age, not because nature ordained it.  Salmond  refines the position — a legal right is ‘an interest recognised and protected by the rule of law’, enforceable by a determinate authority. The criticism is that a purely legal theory leaves the citizen defenceless against an unjust law. 4. Moral and conservative theories.  The  moral  theory ( Kant ,  T.H. Green ) derives rights from the dictates of reason and moral personality — persons must be treated ‘as ends, never merely as means’ — so a right exists wherever it is a condition of moral self-realisation, even if unenforced. The  conservative or historical  theory of  Edmund Burke  grounds rights instead in a long process of  custom  and prescription; he condemned the French Revolution’s ‘metaphysical abstractions’ in favour of ‘the rights of Englishmen’. The standing reply is Indian: custom equally sanctioned sati and untouchability, abolished only by deliberate legislation and Articles 17 and 15. 5. Social-welfare and Marxist theories.  The  social-welfare  theory — Bentham’s utilitarian legacy carried forward by  Roscoe Pound  — holds that rights are justified only in so far as they serve the ‘greatest happiness’ and the common good; critics find the standard vague and majoritarian. The  Marxist  view is sharper: rights are a ‘bourgeois concept’, class law lodged in the superstructure, conferring formal liberty without substantive power — the bonded labourer holds a legal right to freedom yet lacks the means to exercise it, so genuine rights require the abolition of class division. 6. Conclusion.  Laski’s  social-democratic synthesis best reconciles the traditions: rights are rooted in social good yet must secure both individual liberty and social justice, uniting the moral force of natural rights with the enforceability of legal rights. His maxim that ‘every state is known by the rights it maintains’ remains the working test of any regime. Q — Discuss the doctrine of ‘rights as trumps’ (Dworkin) and its critics. Can the right to privacy trump state interest? (UPSC 2019) What it’s asking:  Explain what ‘trumps’ means → apply it to privacy → test it against Dworkin’s own exceptions and his critics. Gist — the spine to recall 1. The doctrine  — individual rights are  ‘trumps’  that beat collective goals, as a trump card beats any other suit.  (Privacy cannot be overridden merely because a database is administratively convenient.)  —  Dworkin ,  Taking Rights Seriously . 2. Anti-utilitarian core  — there is  no easy trade-off  between a right and a policy benefit; rights are not state gifts.  (Majority welfare cannot license torturing one suspect.) 3. Privacy applied  — a right sets the limit policy must respect.  (Puttaswamy, 2017: nine judges read privacy into Art 21, so surveillance must clear legality, necessity and proportionality — not mere ‘security’ assertion.) 4. Dworkin’s own exceptions  — only where the right is at stake in an  attenuated form , or the  cost  is grossly disproportionate.  (Contact-tracing in a pandemic.)  —  Habermas  agrees dignity may be ‘partially defeated’. 5. Critics  — utilitarians deny the priority of rights over aggregate welfare;  Joseph Raz  ( The Authority of Law ) holds law is ‘autonomous’ of morality. 6. Conclusion  — rights are near-absolute, not absolute: a via media between rigid absolutism and utilitarian expediency. Model Answer 1. The doctrine.  In  Taking Rights Seriously ,  Ronald Dworkin  argues that individual rights function as  ‘trumps’  — as a trump card defeats any card of another suit, a right defeats the collective goals of the community or state. Rights are not what the state chooses to grant; on the contrary ‘the sole purpose of the state is the maintenance of rights’. Hence privacy cannot be overridden merely because a centralised database would be administratively convenient. 2. Anti-utilitarian core.  The doctrine is directed against the  positivist and utilitarian  view that a person is entitled only to what the state confers, and that any right may be balanced away once aggregate welfare rises. On the trumps model there is  no easy trade-off : a genuine right cannot be defeated simply because its violation maximises utility, which is why majority benefit cannot license torturing a single suspect. Rights, for Dworkin, express the government’s duty of ‘equal concern and respect’ for each person. 3. Privacy applied.  It follows that  privacy  cannot ordinarily be trumped by a bare appeal to national security or efficiency; the right fixes the boundary within which policy must operate. India supplies the sharpest illustration: in  K.S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India (2017)  a nine-judge Bench held privacy intrinsic to the right to life under Article 21, so state intrusion must satisfy legality, necessity and proportionality. That test is the trumps doctrine in institutional form — the state must justify the intrusion, not the citizen the right. 4. Dworkin’s own exceptions.  Dworkin concedes that a right may be compromised in two narrow cases: first, where the value the right protects is at stake only in some  attenuated form ; and second, where the  cost  of honouring it is grossly disproportionate to its benefit — as with limited disclosure of movement data during an epidemic.  Habermas  reasons similarly that even human dignity, though it normally prevails, may be ‘partially defeated’ in unavoidable circumstances. The exceptions are principled limits, not a general balancing licence. 5. Critics.  Utilitarians reject any lexical priority of rights over aggregate welfare, arguing that Dworkin smuggles in an unargued moral hierarchy.  Joseph Raz , in  The Authority of Law , holds that law is ‘autonomous’ — there is no necessary continuity between legal rights and morality — while communitarians such as  Sandel  and  Walzer  object that the rights-bearing individual is abstracted from the community that gives rights their meaning. 6. Conclusion.  ‘Rights as trumps’ remains the strongest defence of the individual against majoritarian and executive overreach, and it has shaped judicial review far beyond the Anglo-American world. Its qualified exceptions show that even Dworkin treats rights as near-absolute rather than wholly absolute — a via media between rigid absolutism and utilitarian expediency. Q — Can there be a universal conception of human rights? Examine the debate between universalism and cultural relativism. (UPSC 2021) What it’s asking:  State what human rights claim → give the case for universality → present the relativist attack → arrive at a defensible middle position. Gist — the spine to recall 1. What human rights are  — post-1945 claims held by all persons simply as human, codified in the  International Bill of Rights .  (UDHR 1948, drafted in reaction to Nazi atrocities, plus the two 1966 Covenants.) 2. Philosophical basis  —  Locke’s  natural rights plus  Kant’s   human dignity ; the defining claim is  universalism .  (Echoed in the Indian Preamble’s promise of ‘dignity of the individual’.) 3. Case for universality  — a common humanity gives an equal, inalienable claim, and it has abolished manifestly inhuman practices.  (Sati, banned in 1829 after Raja Ram Mohan Roy; female foeticide; genital mutilation — no culture may plead custom.) 4. Relativist challenge  —  cultural relativism  (from  Franz Boas ) and communitarians call universal rights  Western values  in disguise.  (The 1993 Bangkok Declaration’s plea for ‘national and regional peculiarities’; the ‘Asian values’ school.) 5. Value pluralism  —  Isaiah Berlin : values are  incommensurable , so no culture may rank another’s.  (Liberty and equality both matter, yet more of one costs the other.) 6. Conclusion  — a universal  basic minimum , enlarged through  Parekh’s  ‘dialogue among civilisations’, not imposed at gunpoint. Model Answer 1. What human rights are.  Human rights are claims held by every person ‘just because they are human’, irrespective of state, race or creed. They emerged after the Second World War in reaction to the Nazi atrocities and were codified in the  International Bill of Rights  — the  UDHR (1948)  together with the two 1966 Covenants on Civil and Political and on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights. Their novelty lies in piercing sovereignty: how a state treats its own citizens becomes a matter of international concern. 2. Philosophical basis.  Their intellectual pedigree runs from  Locke’s  natural rights — the ‘self-evident truths’ that survive the transfer to civil society — to  Kant’s  conception of  human dignity , by which every person is an end in himself and never merely a means. From this follows their defining and most contested attribute,  universalism : rights are equal, inalienable and permanent. The Indian Preamble’s pledge to secure ‘the dignity of the individual’ shows how deeply the Kantian premise travelled into post-colonial constitutions. 3. The case for universality.  If humanity is one, a claim grounded in humanity alone cannot stop at borders. The practical vindication is that universal standards have delivered where local custom would not: sati, defended as tradition, was banned in 1829 after the campaign of  Raja Ram Mohan Roy ; female foeticide and genital mutilation are today indefensible on cultural grounds; and the corpus keeps expanding, as with the United Nations’ recognition of a human right to water. Without a universal core, the victims of majoritarian custom would have no vocabulary of appeal. 4. The relativist challenge.  Cultural relativists  — the concept descends from the anthropologist  Franz Boas  — hold that every culture is rational on its own terms and that no hierarchy of cultures exists.  Communitarians  add that the self is ‘situated’ and constituted by community, so an abstract rights-bearer is a fiction. Together they charge that ‘universal’ rights are in fact  Western values  universalised — ‘cultural imperialism’. The  Asian values  school of  Lee Kuan Yew  and the  1993 Bangkok Declaration , stressing ‘national and regional peculiarities’, gave the objection diplomatic form. 5. Value pluralism.  Isaiah Berlin  deepens the difficulty: values are genuinely  plural and incommensurable  — liberty and equality are both authentic goods, yet more of one is bought at the cost of the other, and there is ‘no objective criterion’ for ranking them. The West is therefore not entitled to impose its own ordering. Yet Berlin does not collapse into relativism: he retains certain ‘generic values’ common to humanity and prizes  toleration  — Voltaire’s ‘I detest what you say, yet will defend your right to say it’. 6. Conclusion.  A universal conception is defensible, but only as a  basic minimum  of human dignity — against torture, slavery, genocide and arbitrary killing — whose content is enlarged through  Bhikhu Parekh’s  ‘dialogue among civilisations’ rather than imposed ‘at gunpoint’. Human rights should thus be universal in their core and plural in their expression. Q — What do you understand by the three generations of human rights? (UPSC 2018) What it’s asking:  Explain Vasak’s classification generation by generation, and bring out the negative/positive distinction that underlies it. Gist — the spine to recall 1. Origin  —  Karel Vasak  (1979, Strasbourg) classified human rights on the French Revolution’s  liberty, equality, fraternity . 2. First generation — ‘blue’  civil-political rights,  negative : the state must NOT act.  (The state may not censor a newspaper — Art 19(1)(a); ICCPR 1966.) 3. Second generation — ‘red’  socio-economic rights,  positive : the state MUST act and spend.  (The state must provide free schooling to every 6–14 year-old — Art 21A and the RTE Act, 2009; ICESCR 1966.) 4. Third generation — ‘green’  solidarity rights,  collective , exercised in common.  (A healthy environment, development, peace — as in the climate-finance claims of the Global South.) 5. The underlying axis  — negative vs positive rights; welfare states combine both.  (India: enforceable Part III rights beside non-justiciable Part IV directives, later judicially fused through Art 21.) 6. Conclusion  — the generations chart a widening of rights, but the sequence metaphor wrongly implies the later ones are less urgent. Model Answer 1. Origin.  The ‘three generations’ framework was proposed in  1979  by the Czech jurist  Karel Vasak  at the International Institute of Human Rights, Strasbourg. He classified the growing corpus of human rights along the lines of the French Revolution’s slogan ‘liberty, equality, fraternity’, each generation corresponding to a historical phase in which a new kind of claim was pressed and a different demand was made upon the state. 2. First generation — civil and political rights.  Called the  ‘blue rights’ , these are the liberal rights of life, liberty, property, equality before law, freedom of expression, conscience and the vote, recognised in the 1966 Covenant on Civil and Political Rights. They are  negative  in form: they succeed by the state’s  forbearance , not its exertion — the state must NOT censor a newspaper, arrest without warrant or bar a person from a public office. Article 19(1)(a) of the Indian Constitution is enforceable precisely because it demands abstention, which costs the treasury nothing. 3. Second generation — socio-economic and cultural rights.  Called the  ‘red rights’  and championed by socialist states, these cover work, fair wages, social security, health and education, and were recognised in the 1966 Covenant on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights. They are  positive : they require the state to build, employ and spend. India’s Article 21A read with the Right to Education Act, 2009 obliges the state to provide free and compulsory schooling to every child aged six to fourteen — a duty of provision, not of restraint. Both the first and second generations remain  individual-centred . 4. Third generation — solidarity rights.  Called the  ‘green rights’ , these are  collective  claims ‘exercised in solidarity’ — self-determination, peace, development, a healthy environment, humanitarian assistance and a share in the common heritage of mankind. Their bearer is a people rather than a person, and their duty-holder is the international community: the Global South’s demand for climate finance and technology transfer, resting on common but differentiated responsibility, is a third-generation claim in action. 5. The underlying axis.  Cutting across the generations is the  negative–positive  distinction drawn by  Isaiah Berlin  between freedom from interference and freedom to realise oneself. Negative rights are cheap, judicially enforceable and immediate; positive rights are costly, progressive and politically contested. The modern welfare state combines both, and India illustrates the fusion — justiciable fundamental rights in Part III alongside non-justiciable Directive Principles in Part IV, which the Supreme Court has progressively read into Article 21 as rights to livelihood, health and a clean environment. 6. Conclusion.  The generations map the historical widening of rights: from the individual  against  the state, to the individual’s welfare  through  the state, to humanity’s shared claims beyond the state. The metaphor must not be pressed too far, however — treating them as a sequence wrongly implies the later generations are derivative or less urgent, whereas the Vienna Declaration (1993) affirms that all human rights are indivisible and interdependent. Q — Critically examine the ‘Asian values’ critique of human rights and the challenges to their implementation. (UPSC 2016) What it’s asking:  Set out what the Asian-values school claims → explain why enforcement is hard → assess how far the critique holds. Gist — the spine to recall 1. Origin  — a 1990s East Asian assertion rooted in  Confucianism , which prizes harmony and duty over individual claim.  (Singapore’s prosperity-without-dissent model.)  —  Lee Kuan Yew ,  Mahathir Mohamad . 2. Four claims  — rights are not universal; society is  family-centred ; socio-economic rights outrank political ones; and  self-determination  bars outside scrutiny.  (‘Feed the people first, elections later.’) 3. Diplomatic form  — the  1993 Bangkok Declaration  pressed ‘national and regional peculiarities’ before the Vienna World Conference. 4. Reinforcement & reply  — post-colonial thinkers see universal rights as  cultural imperialism ; the West calls Asian values ‘soft authoritarianism’.  (Tiananmen, 1989.) 5. Implementation problem  — rights are  anti-state  yet states are their only guardians, so enforcement means  changing the conduct of states .  (UN bodies can name and shame, but cannot enter a sovereign jurisdiction.) 6. Assessment  —  Amartya Sen : Asia is too diverse for one ‘Asian value’, and freedom is not un-Asian ( The Argumentative Indian ; Ashoka and Akbar on toleration). Model Answer 1. Origin.  The ‘Asian values’ critique arose in the 1990s, after the collapse of the USSR left liberal rights apparently unchallenged and the rise of East Asia supplied a rival model of development. Its principal proponents,  Lee Kuan Yew  of Singapore and  Mahathir Mohamad  of Malaysia, traced their position to  Confucianism , which prizes social harmony, hierarchy and duty to the group above the assertion of individual claims — Singapore’s combination of high prosperity with tightly limited dissent being offered as proof of concept. 2. Four claims.  The school advances four propositions: first, human rights are  not universal  and cannot be globalised, since they grew from a specific Western history; second, Asian societies are centred on the  family and community  rather than the atomised individual; third,  socio-economic rights  — food, housing, employment — rank above political rights for poor societies, so ‘feed the people first, elections later’; and fourth,  national self-determination  includes domestic jurisdiction over one’s human-rights record, so other nations should not interfere. 3. Diplomatic form.  These claims were not merely academic. At the regional meeting preceding the Vienna World Conference on Human Rights, the  1993 Bangkok Declaration  affirmed the universality of human rights in principle while insisting that their implementation ‘must bear in mind the significance of national and regional peculiarities and various historical, cultural and religious backgrounds’ — an attempt to convert cultural relativism into a norm of international law. 4. Reinforcement and reply.  Post-colonial and cultural-relativist thinkers reinforce the critique, reading the universal human-rights regime as  cultural imperialism  — the successor to the civilising mission, now deployed selectively against weaker states. The Western rejoinder is that Asian values amount to ‘soft authoritarianism’: a doctrine articulated by ruling elites rather than by peoples, and used to justify episodes such as the suppression at Tiananmen in 1989 or the silencing of opposition media. 5. The implementation problem.  The deeper difficulty is structural. Human rights are inherently  anti-state  — they are claims against power — yet states remain their principal guardians, so governments offer ‘moral guarantees’ that they routinely fail to honour. Enforcement therefore becomes ‘a matter of  changing the conduct of states ’, which sovereignty, the non-interference claim and the absence of coercive machinery all resist. International bodies can monitor, report and shame; beyond that, compliance depends on domestic courts, a free press and civil society. 6. Assessment.  Amartya Sen  offers the decisive rebuttal: Asia contains sixty per cent of humanity and an immense diversity of traditions, so there is no single ‘Asian value’; and freedom is not un-Asian — in  The Argumentative Indian  he cites Ashoka’s edicts on toleration and Akbar’s  sulh-i-kul  as indigenous roots of liberty. The critique rightly warns against ethnocentric imposition, but hardens into a shield for authoritarian denial; the way forward is a negotiated basic minimum, monitored internationally yet advanced through dialogue rather than coercion. Q — Discuss multiculturalism and minority rights, with special reference to Kymlicka and Bhikhu Parekh. What it’s asking:  Explain why equal treatment may require unequal rights → give Kymlicka’s and Parekh’s schemes → weigh the feminist and liberal objections. Gist — the spine to recall 1. Origin  — grew out of the liberal–communitarian debate: identity is culturally embedded, so identical treatment can entrench disadvantage.  (A uniform dress code silently excludes a turbaned Sikh.) 2. Kymlicka’s liberal defence  — a secure culture is the precondition of  individual autonomy ; being born a minority is ‘bad brute luck’ deserving rectification ( Multicultural Citizenship ). 3. Three group-differentiated rights  —  polyethnic  ( Arts 29–30: minorities may run their own schools ),  special representation  ( SC/ST seats under Arts 330 and 332 ),  self-government  ( the Fifth and Sixth Schedules’ autonomous tribal councils ) — but only for national minorities. 4. Parekh’s dialogical view  — multiculturalism is the ‘creative interplay’ of embeddedness and plurality; universal norms must emerge through  dialogue among civilisations  ( Rethinking Multiculturalism ). 5. Critiques  —  Okin : ‘multiculturalism is bad for women’  (personal laws can shield unequal maintenance or inheritance) ;  Sen  and  Barry  fear ghettoisation. 6. Conclusion  — accommodate difference, but bound it by a basic minimum of individual rights. Model Answer 1. Origin.  Multiculturalism emerged from the  liberal–communitarian debate  of the 1980s to defend the claims of  minority cultures . Its premise is that culture is constitutive of identity and of the range of options from which a person chooses, so a formally neutral rule may in practice impose the majority’s culture — a uniform dress code or a Sunday holiday silently excludes the turbaned Sikh or the observant minority worker. Treating people as equals may therefore require not identical but  group-specific  rights. 2. Kymlicka’s liberal defence.  Will Kymlicka , in  Multicultural Citizenship , argues that liberalism itself requires the protection of minority cultures, because a secure ‘societal culture’ is the context within which meaningful choice, and hence  individual autonomy , is possible. Being born into a vulnerable minority culture is ‘bad brute luck’ rather than a chosen disadvantage, and on his  luck-egalitarian  premise the state owes its rectification. Multiculturalism is thus a completion of liberalism, not a departure from it. 3. Three group-differentiated rights.  Kymlicka grants three classes of  group-differentiated rights .  Polyethnic rights  protect distinctive religious and cultural practice — Articles 29 and 30 of the Indian Constitution permit minorities to conserve their script and to establish and administer their own educational institutions.  Special representation rights  secure a political voice, as with reserved seats for Scheduled Castes and Tribes under Articles 330 and 332.  Self-government rights  grant territorial autonomy, exemplified by the Fifth and Sixth Schedules with their autonomous district councils in the North-East. Crucially, he reserves the last for ‘national minorities’ incorporated involuntarily, not for voluntary immigrants. 4. Parekh’s dialogical view.  Bhikhu Parekh , in  Rethinking Multiculturalism , takes a post-colonial position: multiculturalism is the ‘creative interplay’ of cultural embeddedness and human plurality, and no culture is complete in itself. He finds no logic in denying special rights to non-citizen minorities, applies a  harm principle  to test contested cultural practices rather than banning them wholesale, and insists that universal principles must be constructed through  dialogue among civilisations , anchored in the shared value of  human dignity . 5. Critiques.  Feminists warn that protecting cultures can entrench patriarchy:  Susan Moller Okin’s  ‘multiculturalism is bad for women’ argues that group rights typically empower male elders, and India’s personal-law debates over maintenance and inheritance illustrate the risk of internal minorities being sacrificed to external protection. Liberals such as  Amartya Sen  and  Brian Barry  fear ‘ghettoisation’ and ‘plural monoculturalism’ — communities living side by side rather than together — with a corresponding weakening of shared citizenship. 6. Conclusion.  Multiculturalism corrects the blindness of abstract equal treatment and is indispensable in deeply diverse societies such as India. But it must be bounded: group rights are legitimate as external protections against majority pressure, not as internal restrictions on dissenting members, so cultural accommodation must stop at the basic minimum of individual human rights. Q — Assess the significance of the right to property in political theory. (UPSC 2020) What it’s asking:  Trace why property is the most contested right — the liberal defence, the socialist attack, the social-liberal balance — and what its Indian career proves. Gist — the spine to recall 1. Why contested  — property sits at the crossroads of  liberty and equality : securing one man’s freedom can entrench another’s subordination.  (Zamindari: title for one, tenancy for millions.) 2. Classical debate  —  Plato  saw it as corrupting (communism of the guardians),  Aristotle  as a school of virtue;  Machiavelli : men ‘sooner forget the death of a father than the loss of patrimony’. 3. Liberal defence  —  Locke : a  natural right  earned by mixing labour with nature;  Smith  and  Bentham : the engine of incentive and progress.  (Secure land titles raise investment.) 4. Socialist critique  — private (productive) property is the basis of  class division , exploitation and alienation;  Proudhon : ‘property is theft’. 5. Social-liberal balance  — property has a  social origin  and must serve the common good ( Laski, Hobhouse ); Gandhian  trusteeship  makes the owner a custodian. 6. The Indian verdict  — the  44th Amendment (1978)  deleted Art 31 and demoted property from a  fundamental  to a  legal  right (Art 300A) so land reform could proceed — property is conditional, not absolute. Model Answer 1. Why it is contested.  Few rights have divided political theory as sharply as the right to property, precisely because it stands at the crossroads of  liberty and equality . As a bulwark of independence it shields the individual from the state; as an accumulation of power it reproduces inequality across generations. Colonial India furnishes the illustration: the permanent settlement created secure proprietary title for the zamindar and precarious tenancy for millions, so the same right simultaneously guaranteed freedom and entrenched subordination. 2. The classical debate.  Plato  regarded property as a source of corruption and faction, and abolished it for the guardian class so that rulers might have no private interest distinct from the city’s.  Aristotle  replied that private ownership is a school of virtue — it teaches prudence, liberality and responsibility, and what is common to all is cared for by none.  Machiavelli  added the political observation that men ‘sooner forget the death of their father than the loss of their patrimony’, warning princes never to touch their subjects’ possessions. 3. The liberal defence.  John Locke  made property a  natural right  antecedent to government: by mixing his labour with nature a man makes a thing his own, and the protection of ‘lives, liberties and estates’ is the very end for which the state is instituted — the core of what  Macpherson  called ‘possessive individualism’.  Adam Smith  and  Bentham  defended it on utilitarian grounds as the indispensable engine of incentive, security and social progress, an argument echoed today in evidence that secure land titling raises investment. 4. The socialist critique.  For  Marxists , private property in the means of production is the very  basis of class division , generating exploitation through surplus value and the alienation of the worker from his product, his labour and himself; they carefully distinguish personal from productive property, abolishing only the latter.  Proudhon’s  aphorism ‘property is theft’ compresses the charge, and  Rousseau  had already traced civil inequality to the first man who enclosed a plot and said ‘this is mine’. 5. The social-liberal balance.  Laski , in  A Grammar of Politics , treats property as an instrument of the  common good  rather than an absolute claim, while  Hobhouse  stresses its  social origin  — no fortune is the product of one man’s effort alone, since it presupposes law, infrastructure and society’s cooperation, which justifies taxation and redistribution.  Sen  and  Dworkin  tie its allocation to justice, and the Gandhian doctrine of  trusteeship  makes the owner a custodian holding wealth for society. 6. The Indian verdict and conclusion.  India’s constitutional history is the clearest practical judgment on the question. Property began as a fundamental right under Articles 19(1)(f) and 31, but the collision between land reform and compensation produced a long duel between Parliament and the Supreme Court, resolved by the  44th Amendment (1978) , which deleted Article 31 and relocated property as a  legal  right under  Article 300A . The significance of the right to property therefore lies in this unresolved tension — indispensable to individual freedom yet dangerous to equality — which is why the modern welfare state treats it not as absolute but as socially conditioned.
